newsitem.title: USA: Independent filmmakers trumpet Oscar successes.
newsitem.headline: Independent filmmakers trumpet Oscar successes.

text.p: Independent filmmakers were quick to cash in on their most triumphant Oscar night ever on Tuesday, leaving the major studios in the embarrassing position of having virtually nothing to boast about.

"Winner 9 Academy Awards" screamed the large ad in the Los Angeles Times for Miramax's "The English Patient," which won for best picture, best director and best supporting actress among the accolades heaped on it at Monday night's glittering Academy Awards presentation.

While the results of the 69th Academy Awards came too late to get advertisements in east coast newspapers because of the three-hour time difference -- the ceremony finished about 12:30 a.m. EST (0530 GMT) on Tuesday -- the independent filmmakers made hay on the west coast.
"Academy Award Winner Best Actor Geoffrey Rush" shouted out the Times ad for "Shine," produced by Fine Line Features.
Similar adds touted the success stories of "Sling Blade," also from Miramax, which garnered a best adapted screenplay for the movie's star, Billy Bob Thornton.
The success of the independent filmmakers left most of the larger studios virtually empty-handed Monday.

Only Sony Corp's TriStar could bask in the glow of Cuba Gooding Jr's best supporting actor Oscar for "Jerry Maguire". However, industry giants Walt Disney Co and Time Warner Inc could take some solace in the fact that their independent studio divisions managed to succeed where they had failed.
Disney owns Miramax, which produced "The English Patient", "Sling Blade," and "Emma" while Time Warner owns Fine Line Features, grabbed the best acting Oscar for "Shine"

While "The English Patient," reportedly made on a moderate budget of about $30 million, could never be called a blockbuster movie, it is still among the top 10 box office draws after 19 weeks in release and has so far taken in $63 million in the United States alone. Hollywood publicist and Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences member Dick Delson expects that to at least double following the film's Oscar success.
"I expect 'Patient' to continue to be a box office draw here, it will do very well in Europe and down the line it will have terrific video sales," he said.

Delson said academy members could be quirky in their Oscar voting and the fact that the small filmmakers declared "Independents Day" on Monday did not necessarily bode ill for the big studios on future award nights.
"The academy members chose to go with the independents this year, but the big studios could come back next year and have a banner Oscar year," he said.

If Monday's results came in too late for advertisements in newspapers in some of the major markets, the independent films got plenty of free publicity on television with Tuesday's morning news and talk shows being dominated by who won what, who wore what or who did what at the Oscars.

While "The English Patient" was definitely the flavor of the night, it fell short of matching the record 11 wins earned by the 1959 film "Ben-Hur" starring Charlton Heston, who also won an Oscar for the lead role.
Still, the place to be in the wee hours of Tuesday morning was the plush Mondrian Hotel in Hollywood, practically taken over by Miramax in anticipation of a big night.

Even the fact that "The English Patient," a romance set in the Second World War, managed only one of the four acting category awards -- a best supporting actress Oscar for French-born Juliette Binoche -- did not stop the champagne from flowing.
In a year when major studios took a back seat to obscure independents, Oscar host Billy Crystal echoed the question that every TV viewer asked: "Who are these people?"

Such was the dominance of "The English Patient" that Andrew Lloyd Webber, collecting his Oscar for best song, "You Must Love Me," from "Evita," echoed the sentiments of many nominees when he said, "Thank heavens there wasn't a song in 'The English Patient' is all I can say."

In addition to best picture and Anthony Minghella's best director award for the "The English Patient," as well as Binoche's Oscar, the film also garnered Oscars for art direction, cinematography, costume design, film editing, original dramatic score and sound.
Frances McDormand took best actress for her portrayal of a pregnant police chief in the gritty crime drama "Fargo," another independent production, by Gramercy films.
